meta.description: Credited to JFK's State of the Union — but the line is missing from the official text and recording, surviving only in a period Vital Speeches and Documents of the Day printing.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'A child miseducated is a child lost'?
meta.ogDescription: Yes, it's Kennedy — from the 1962 State of the Union. But the exact line isn't in the official text or the recording, only a period print version.

answer.label: Attributed to
answer.sourceLine: Widely and consistently credited to Kennedy’s 1962 State of the Union Address (11 January 1962), and fully consistent with that speech’s education section. The exact wording survives in a period printing in Vital Speeches and Documents of the Day, Vol. 2 (1961), but it does not appear in the official text of the address or in the audio/video recording — so genuine authorship is likely, yet the precise line can’t be pinned to an authoritative primary source as delivered.

source.excerpt: A child miseducated is a child lost.
trail: The line is credited to Kennedy across virtually every quote database, from Goodreads to BrainyQuote, usually pinned to a “1963 State of the Union” with no exact source.

The quotations-research site WIST traces it instead to the 1962 State of the Union, noting it is absent from the formal text and recording but shows up in a copy printed in Vital Speeches and Documents of the Day, Vol. 2 (1961) — possibly a press-release or reading-copy variant.

The official transcript at the American Presidency Project confirms the exact line does not appear as delivered, though the address’s education passage — on illiteracy and unequal access to schooling — carries the same idea.
source.excerptNote: No reliable surrounding sentence exists in the official record: the phrase is missing from the delivered text of the 1962 State of the Union and from the audio/video, appearing only in a secondary print version of the speech that also carries other small textual differences.

source.rightsNote: A U.S. President’s State of the Union Address is a work of the U.S. Government and is not subject to copyright, so the 1962 speech text is public domain regardless of which printing carries the exact line. Note this is a rights judgment about the underlying government speech, separate from the open question of whether Kennedy delivered this precise wording.

author.name: John F. Kennedy
author.heading: About John F. Kennedy
author.bio: John Fitzgerald Kennedy served as the 35th President of the United States from 1961 until his assassination in 1963. His administration pressed hard on federal aid to education, making schools, teacher pay, and literacy recurring themes of his major addresses. His State of the Union messages and speeches, as official presidential acts, are public-domain U.S. Government works.

misattribution.heading: The source problem
misattribution.intro: This one isn’t a case of the wrong author — it’s a case of the wrong (or missing) source. The line is genuinely Kennedy-flavored, but it circulates with a citation that doesn’t hold up.

items.why: The most common tag points to the 1963 address, where the phrase does not appear at all. WIST re-traces it to the 1962 address instead.
The phrase is absent from the official transcript at the American Presidency Project and from the audio/video recording; it survives only in a secondary print version of the speech.

misattribution.truthLine: Best read as a genuine but unverifiable Kennedy line: consistent with his 1962 education message and documented in a period printing, but not confirmed in any authoritative primary source as delivered — see WIST’s source note.

context.heading: Why it resonates
lead: Kennedy’s 1962 State of the Union pushed federal support for schools, teacher salaries, and college access, framing education as a matter of national strength. He warned that “eight million adult Americans are classified as functionally illiterate” and argued that every able high-school graduate deserved the chance to develop their talents.
“A child miseducated is a child lost” distills that argument into a single line — which is exactly why it spread, and why its murky sourcing rarely gets questioned.
context.pull: Not the wrong author — the wrong source.
